name: Samba Batucada (full bateria)
desc: The driving Rio escola de samba groove felt in 2, with the surdo answering on beats 2 and 4 and syncopated caixa/tamborim sixteenths on top. The foundation of carnival batucada.

name: Surdo de Primeira (Surdo 1 marcação)
desc: The lowest surdo marks the strongest beat (beat 4, the 'two' of the 2/4 samba) with an open ringing tone, anchoring the bateria's pulse.

name: Surdo de Segunda (Surdo 2 marcação)
desc: The mid surdo answers the first surdo, marking beat 2 (the 'one' of samba's two-feel) with an open tone, completing the heartbeat call-and-response of the surdos.

name: Surdo de Terceira (Surdo 3 corte)
desc: The cutting third surdo improvises syncopated fills between the marking surdos, adding the floating off-beat phrases characteristic of Rio escolas.

name: Tamborim Teleco-teco
desc: The classic teleco-teco tamborim phrase that gives samba its melodic syncopation, accenting just ahead of and around the surdo beats.

name: Caixa Samba (continuous sixteenths)
desc: The snare-drum caixa lays a constant carpet of sixteenths with accents on the 'e' of each beat, giving samba its swinging forward drive.

name: Repinique Chamada (call)
desc: The repinique leads the bateria, sounding the chamada that signals entries and breaks with sharp ringing strokes around the beat.

name: Samba de Enredo
desc: The grand parade samba of the escolas, a theme-song groove built for thousands of dancers, with surdos marking 2 and 4 and dense syncopated upper percussion.

name: Partido Alto
desc: A call-and-response samba subgenre whose signature pandeiro/clave phrase emphasizes the off-beats, the rhythmic backbone of roda-de-samba improvisation.

name: Samba de Roda
desc: The ancestral circle samba of the Bahian Recôncavo, played on pandeiro, atabaque and palmas, recognized by UNESCO as a root of all samba.

name: Pagode
desc: The intimate backyard samba style of the 1980s, lighter and more melodic, driven by tantã, repique de mão and pandeiro with a relaxed swing.

name: Samba-Canção
desc: A slow, romantic ballad form of samba where the percussion thins to a gentle marking of 2 and 4, emphasizing the melody and lyrics.

name: Samba Cruzado (drum kit)
desc: The drum-set adaptation of samba where the bass drum plays the surdo-derived crossed pattern and the left foot keeps 2 and 4 on the hi-hat.

name: Bossa Nova
desc: The cool, understated cousin of samba born on Rio's beaches, with a soft surdo-style bass drum and a cross-stick rim clave evoking the bossa guitar.

name: Bossa Nova Clave (forward)
desc: The two-bar bossa nova rim-click clave (3-2 forward direction) that João Gilberto distilled from samba, the rhythmic signature of the genre.

name: Choro
desc: Brazil's first urban instrumental genre, propelled by pandeiro and the syncopated baixaria of the seven-string guitar, ancestor of samba and instrumental virtuosity.

name: Choro Pandeiro
desc: The pandeiro pattern that drives choro, alternating thumb bass tones on the beats with fingertip and slap accents filling the sixteenths.

name: Maxixe
desc: The 'Brazilian tango' of the late 1800s that fused habanera and lundu into a syncopated couple dance, a direct forerunner of samba.

name: Lundu
desc: The Afro-Brazilian song-and-dance of Angolan/Bantu origin built on a habanera-like syncopation, the earliest African-rooted music accepted into Brazilian salons.

name: Baião
desc: The foundational Northeastern rhythm popularized by Luiz Gonzaga, with its signature zabumba figure (low boom on the beat, accent on the 'a') under constant triangle sixteenths.

name: Baião Zabumba (full)
desc: The two-headed zabumba groove of baião: muffled low boom on beat 1, damped high slap from the bacalhau stick on the off-beats, under a shimmering triangle.

name: Forró
desc: The pan-Northeastern dance music descended from baião, identified by the zabumba's open low sound on the last sixteenth of the bar that pulls into the next measure.

name: Xote
desc: The slower, swaying Northeastern partner dance derived from the European schottische, marked by the zabumba's open low tones on the two eighths of the second beat.

name: Xaxado
desc: The marching sertão dance of the cangaceiros from the Pernambuco backlands, named for the shuffling 'xa-xa' of sandals, driven by a steady zabumba march.

name: Arrasta-pé
desc: The fast, festive June-festival forró variant whose name means 'drag the foot', pushing the baião feel to a punchy quick tempo for São João dancing.

name: Coco
desc: The coastal Northeastern song-and-dance built on stamped feet, hand-claps and the ganzá, a call-and-response form tied to coconut-breaking work songs.

name: Embolada
desc: The rapid-fire tongue-twisting vocal genre of coco, where pandeiro keeps a relentless even sixteenth pulse under improvised, competitive sung verses.

name: Ciranda
desc: The Pernambuco coastal circle dance played on mineiro, bombo and ganzá, a slow swaying 2-feel that draws dancers into a giant ring on the beach.

name: Frevo
desc: The frenetic Pernambuco carnival march of Recife and Olinda, a fast brass-band style with snappy syncopated snare accents that fuel the acrobatic passo dance.

name: Maracatu Nação (Baque Virado)
desc: The thunderous 'turned beat' processional from Recife-Olinda, with interlocking alfaia drums answering the mestre's call and the gonguê bell marking the timeline.

name: Maracatu Gonguê Timeline
desc: The gonguê cowbell timeline that is the spine of baque virado, its asymmetric bell phrase locking the alfaias and caixas of the nação together.

name: Maracatu Rural (Baque Solto)
desc: The 'loose beat' of the Zona da Mata sugarcane region, a frenetic style with rolling tarol/caixa, mineiro and brass behind the spinning caboclo de lança.

name: Afoxé (Ijexá)
desc: The Candomblé-rooted carnival rhythm of Salvador's blocos afro, built on the ijexá agogô bell pattern with atabaques and xequerê at a gently rolling tempo.

name: Ijexá Agogô Bell
desc: The two-tone agogô ostinato of ijexá, the sacred bell timeline that underlies afoxé and feeds directly into the accents of samba-reggae.

name: Samba-Reggae (Olodum)
desc: The signature bloco-afro groove of Salvador created by Neguinho do Samba and Olodum, reorienting samba's surdos around a reggae backbeat with the famous syncopated surdo answer.

name: Samba-Reggae Surdo Interlock
desc: The four-surdo interlocking pyramid of samba-reggae, where surdos 1-4 each take a slice of the bar to build the rolling Olodum wall of low drums.

name: Timbalada (Timbau groove)
desc: Carlinhos Brown's Bahian style played on the conical hand-drum timbau, blending samba-reggae and Candomblé into a dense, bass-heavy carnival groove.

name: Axé
desc: The pop-carnival music of Salvador's trio elétrico era, fusing afoxé, frevo and samba-reggae into an upbeat, danceable backbeat-driven sound.

name: Carimbó
desc: The Afro-Indigenous drum-and-dance music of Pará in the Amazon, played on large hollowed-log carimbó drums with maracas, ancestor of lambada.

name: Marcha (Marchinha de Carnaval)
desc: The bouncy two-beat carnival march of early-20th-century Rio, with an oom-pah bass on every beat and a singalong melody, the sound of old-school Brazilian Carnaval.

name: Capoeira Toque Angola
desc: The slow, low, grounded berimbau toque for the traditional capoeira Angola game, calling players to a crafty, close-to-the-ground jogo with pandeiro and atabaque.

name: Capoeira Toque São Bento Grande
desc: The fast, driving berimbau toque of capoeira Regional created by Mestre Bimba, energizing an athletic, fast-paced game in the roda.

name: Capoeira Toque São Bento Pequeno
desc: A medium-tempo berimbau toque whose low note falls on the off-beat, often paired with São Bento Grande to layer the gunga and viola berimbaus.

name: Capoeira Toque Iúna
desc: Mestre Bimba's berimbau toque imitating the call-and-response song of the iúna bird, reserved for graduated capoeiristas playing a refined, acrobatic game without singing.

name: Capoeira Toque Benguela
desc: A slow, hypnotic berimbau toque (associated with Mestre Pastinha) for a malicious, deceptive low game, swaying between the open and pressed notes.

name: Capoeira Toque Cavalaria
desc: The berimbau toque imitating galloping mounted police, historically a coded warning in the roda that the cavalry was approaching to raid the capoeira game.

name: Capoeira Toque Santa Maria
desc: A berimbau toque traditionally used for the jogo de dentro and money-grabbing games (jogo do dinheiro), with a distinctive answered low phrase.

name: Capoeira Toque Samango
desc: A regional berimbau toque used in some capoeira lineages for a flowing, mid-tempo game, varying the placement of the pressed buzz note.

name: Candomblé Ijexá (atabaque)
desc: The sacred Candomblé toque for Oxum and other orixás, a calm rolling ijexá played on rum, rumpi and lê atabaques with the agogô, parent of afoxé.

name: Candomblé Vassi
desc: A foundational Ketu Candomblé toque in 12 pulses with seven hand-drum strokes spread across the cycle, used in many orixá ceremonies.

name: Candomblé Aguerê
desc: The compound-time toque for the warrior-hunter orixá Oxóssi, a galloping 12/8 atabaque rhythm evoking the chase through the forest.

name: Candomblé Opanijé
desc: The stately 16-pulse toque for Obaluaiê/Omolu, the orixá of disease and healing, with a deliberate limping phrase that mirrors the orixá's dance.

name: Candomblé Barravento
desc: A fast, accelerating Candomblé toque used to call the orixás into possession (the 'turning of the wind'), driving the rum's improvisations to a peak.

name: Candomblé Alujá (Xangô)
desc: The vigorous toque dedicated to Xangô, orixá of thunder and justice, a fast atabaque rhythm whose rolling rum phrases evoke crashing thunder.

name: Congado (Congada)
desc: The Afro-Brazilian Catholic processional of Minas Gerais honoring Our Lady of the Rosary, with caixas and patangome bells marching the crowned-king cortege.

name: Catira (Cateretê)
desc: The caipira foot-stomping and hand-clapping dance of Brazil's rural interior, where dancers' palmas and sapateado create the percussion alongside the viola.

name: Baile Funk Tamborzão
desc: The defining Rio funk carioca beat built from sampled atabaque/conga hits, a syncopated surdo-like kick with tight claps on 2 and 4, descended from Candomblé and capoeira drums.

name: Baile Funk (Volt Mix / Miami bass)
desc: The earlier Miami-bass-derived funk carioca groove (the '808 Volt mix' break) that founded the genre in 1980s Rio before tamborzão, with electro kick and clap.

name: Maculelê
desc: The Afro-Brazilian stick-dance from Bahia performed with clashing grimas, accompanied by atabaque and song, often shown alongside capoeira.

name: Tambor de Crioula
desc: The Afro-Maranhão circle dance honoring São Benedito, played on three hand drums (tambor grande, meião, crivador) with the navel-bump punga, UNESCO heritage.

name: Jongo (Caxambu)
desc: The Bantu-rooted drum-and-dance of the Paraíba Valley played on tambu and candongueiro drums, a riddle-song tradition counted among samba's ancestors.

name: Maracatu Baque de Marcação
desc: The steady marking baque of maracatu nação used to move the cortege between viradas, with alfaias and gonguê holding a walking processional pulse.

name: Samba-Funk (Samba Afro)
desc: The Bahian bloco-afro fusion of samba-reggae with funk and Candomblé, a heavy surdo groove with a backbeat snare championed by groups like Ilê Aiyê.

name: Pagode Baiano
desc: The fast Salvador dance-music offshoot of axé and samba-reggae driven by timbau and percussion, propelling the energetic swingueira choreography.
